events.text:
This is game 96 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:
- CLAUDE.md (138,992 bytes)
- count.py (828 bytes)
- libs.py (1,378 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

D9 adds a liberty but still leaves me around three in a tight race with black's chain. F7 extends toward G7 but drags me into black's area with uncertain gains.

Looking at black's center chain through D6 and E4-E6, it only has four liberties; if I play F6 I'd cut that down to three, though F6 doesn't directly connect to my E7 group since it's diagonal.

I'm reconsidering eye shape around D9-E8-E9-F8-F9 for my top group, but with black's G7 nearby that space looks cramped. Let me try B7 as the key connecting point and read out the sequence: after black plays D9 my top group drops to just E8, F7 liberties, dangerous, so I'd need to respond with E8 to get back to three liberties while black continues pressing.

Alternatively I could just play E8 now for better shape, giving me four liberties, then let black connect at B7 forming their own group with five liberties. My top group would still need to make eyes near D9/E9/F8/F9 with some risk from black's G7 stone nearby, but it should live small. Roughly totaling up territory, black likely takes a small top-left corner while I get a bigger right side plus some bottom-left area.

I think cutting at B7 first is actually the sharper move — it fights the connection directly rather than letting black link up cheaply. If black responds at D9 after my B7, I need to check whether E9 or A6 gives me the better follow-up to keep my group's liberties ahead while threatening the C-chain.

Tracing this further, black still comes out ahead in the liberty race after E9, so that line looks too risky. If I give up D7-D8-E7, black takes top-left and top while I only get the bottom-left, which puts me around 22 and clearly losing — so the top fight really matters. Reconsidering D9 for my group: extending to D7-E7-D8-D9 gives me three liberties, but the black chain still has four and likely lives in the corner with eye space, so killing it looks unlikely; maybe F7 is the better continuation.

Checking the shape with D7-E7-F7-D8, I get four liberties and F7 also pressures G7 and the black center chain, while black D9 would only leave black with three liberties, which isn't an improvement for them. In the end I'll just go with B7 — it's a fighting chance since the black C-chain's eye space is so small, even though my top group is a bit thin at three liberties. B7 it is.
